the full-length E2-encoding sequence is a reliable tool for molecular epidemiology and tracing of classical swine Fever virus.
the full-length E2 gene (1119 nt, 374 amino acids, aa) is most suitable for phylogenetic studies of CSFV.

the full-length E2 coding sequence is the best suited for reliable and statistically valid phylogenetic analyses and that the E2 gene is therefore recommended as the most appropriate target for CSF molecular epidemiology.

the optimization of CSFV molecular phylogenetics.
the development of a more reliable and efficient strategy for molecular tracing and epidemiology of CSFV.
the development of a new strategy for CSFV phylogenetic analysis and provides the first detailed comparison of different CSFV sequence fragments with respect to their suitability for this purpose.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
full-length E2 sequences are the best option for phylogenetic and molecular epidemiological analysis of classical swines fever virus.
the full-length E2 sequences are the best sequences for molecular epidemiological analysis of CSFV, but that also the 5´UTR sequences can provide reliable results.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the full-length E2 gene encoding sequence (1119 nt, GenBank accession number JQ682433) is a reliable and powerful tool in CSFV molecular diagnostics and epidemiology.
the E2 region of the CSFV genome can be considered as the most suitable marker region for molecular epidemiological investigations.
the 5´-NTR-E2 fragment (190 nt), which is the most frequently used fragment in phylogenetic studies of CSFV, should be replaced with the full-length E2 sequence (1119 nt).
The main takeaway from our work is that
phylogenetic analysis based on full-length sequences of E2 is a reliable tool in molecular epidemiology and that it provides a more accurate basis for CSF control measures.
the full-length E2 gene is a suitable marker for molecular epidemiological studies of CSFV.
the use of the E2 gene for phylogenetic and evolutionary analysis of CSFV is superior to other genomic regions.
